title: MIPLIB 2010
contribution: Infrastructure for MIP benchmarking: a 361-instance library of purpose-specific test sets with entry rules, an exact-arithmetic solution checker, a test engine, a per-instance variability score and a five-solver snapshot that declines to rank (pp. 1-2).
problem_entry: MIPLIB 2003 had been solved down (Fig. 1, p. 3), topic subsets gave inadequate test sets and tuning was biased toward solvable models (p. 4); stated as a community need (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A library of eight purpose-specific test sets with stated entry rules (Table 1, p. 5), shipped with a test engine and exact checker (pp. 8-13), variability measured per instance (pp. 13-18) and a non-ranking snapshot (pp. 46-56).
assumptions: MILP in MPS, whose 12-character fields and tolerances make the solved region a perturbation (pp. 9-10); mostly binary, sparse instances (pp. 43, 45); set entry thresholds are environment-dependent guiding values (pp. 5-8).
proof_devices: exact rational (GMP) feasibility checker on the MPS text, tolerances 1e-4 / 1e-7 (pp. 10-11)
gap definition monotone in both bounds with undefined cases listed (p. 11)
solver and solution status scheme incl. mismatch against reliable primal bounds (pp. 11-12)
run.sh/parse.awk per-solver script layout (pp. 12-13)
reliable primal values by fixing rounded integers and exact LP re-solve with QSopt_ex (pp. 12, 43)
variability score: coefficient of variation of time over permutations (pp. 14-15)
attention level from basis condition histogram (pp. 43-44)
experiments: Staged benchmark selection from about 2,000 candidates (p. 6); five-solver snapshot at 1 and 12 threads with per-instance tables (pp. 46-55); noise checks on a second machine and repeated deterministic runs (p. 51); 100 permutations per model with scip/spx, ratios 1.29 to 915, oracles 1.77 and 3.82 (pp. 15-18).
positioning: MIPLIB lineage 1992, 1996, 2003 (p. 2); variability credited to Danna, measure changed to time (pp. 13-15); performance profiles and inferential statistics pointed to but not used (p. 18); critique aimed at topic subsets and single-number rankings (pp. 4, 51, 56).
writing: Collective we; motivating speedup numbers qualified at once (pp. 3-4); hedges on variability (pp. 14-15); section 7 disclaims a ranking before the table and lists reasons after (pp. 46, 51, 56); ends on a methodological lesson (p. 56).
limits_future: Thresholds environment-dependent (p. 7), variability score a sample estimate (p. 15), attention level algorithm-dependent (p. 44), exact MIP cannot certify most optima (p. 43), limited time for challenge set (p. 43); open questions on variability (p. 14).

method_links.note: Co-signed: the instrument comes with the data (run scripts, parser per solver, checker, reliable primal bounds); step 2 of Method 5 and Heuristic 4 at library scale. Variant within it: instances chosen with current developer versions, not a frozen older version as in step 5 (pp. 6-7).

Co-signed: contradicts step 7 and Misreading 1; samples 100 permutations per model, prints a variability score per benchmark instance and recommends permuted copies, robust statistics and inferential tests. Qualifier: 16 authors, section rests on Danna's work; the rest matches Method 4's reading rules (pp. 46, 51, 56).
Variability measured in solve time, not simplex iterations, since iterations are not comparable across codes and much MIP work is not simplex.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: one number per model and solver, with the sampling protocol and the censoring stated, and stable instances favoured in the benchmark

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: purpose-specific test sets with rule-based membership
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: eight sets with stated entry rules

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: certify only what can be certified
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: feasibility checked in exact arithmetic, and primal values made reliable by an exact LP re-solve
the reasons given are variability, arbitrary limits, per-instance ratios above 1,000 and measures that change the winner

transferable: Benchmark entry rules as measurable thresholds: iterations per node, tree size, problem size, root bound equal to the optimum. Label them as guiding values and cross-check membership on several codes and machines (p. 7).
Per-instance variability score: the coefficient of variation of time over many permutations, with the time limit stated and limit-affected scores flagged (pp. 14–15).
To show skew, report the best and worst permutation oracles (1.77 and 3.82) and compare the original run with both the mean and the median (14 % against 4 %) (pp. 15–16).
Check returned solutions in exact arithmetic against the original text file, with separate tolerances for constraints, integrality and the objective (pp. 10–11).
Make primal bounds reliable by fixing the rounded integers and solving the remaining LP exactly (pp. 12, 43).
Before trusting a timing difference, rerun on a second machine and repeat deterministic parallel runs. Here that moved geometric means by 8.5–20 % and single runs by up to 73 s (p. 51).
A gap definition that is monotone and bounds the relative gap, with its undefined cases written out (p. 11).
coauthors: Thorsten Koch, Erling Andersen, Oliver Bastert, Timo Berthold, Robert E. Bixby, Emilie Danna, Gerald Gamrath, Ambros M. Gleixner, Stefan Heinz, Andrea Lodi, Hans D. Mittelmann, Ted K. Ralphs, Domenico Salvagnin, Daniel E. Steffy, Kati Wolter

title: Rounding and Propagation Heuristics for Mixed Integer Programming
contribution: An overview of SCIP's cheap rounding and propagation heuristics together with a new measure, the primal integral, and a four-setting evaluation design (pp. 3, 5-7).
problem_entry: A measurement gap: usual measures do not capture the speed/solution-quality trade-off of early solutions (pp. 3, 5); scope limited to cheap rounding and propagation heuristics (abstract, p. 3).
key_idea: (i) Overview of seven lock-based heuristics (pp. 4-5); (ii) the primal integral P(T) of the primal gap step function, read as average incumbent quality (pp. 5-6).
assumptions: MIP min c^T x, Ax <= b, bounds, integrality (p. 3); locks presume rows in <= form (p. 4); primal gap needs an optimal or best known solution and a fixed environment (p. 6); 82 MIPLIB 2010 benchmark instances (p. 6).
proof_devices: Simple Rounding lock-based safety rule (p. 4)
Rounding with locks as tie-breaker (p. 4)
ZI Round largest LP-feasible shift (p. 4)
Shifting with non-improving-shift stop (pp. 4-5)
Shift-and-Propagate fixing order and postponement (p. 5)
Oneopt and Twoopt improvement shifts (p. 5)
primal gap, p(t), P(T) definitions eqs. (2)-(4) (pp. 5-6)
normalisation of P(t_max) by the all-heuristics-off run (p. 7)
experiments: Four SCIP settings (Heur OFF, R&P, NoR&P, DEF), 1 h, 4 GB, one machine, no version, seeds or repeats (p. 6); phi(P) 0.44/0.47/0.61/1.0 and solve-time loss printed (Table 1, p. 7); the card's recount finds 13 of 82 instances where DEF worsens the integral (pp. 9-18).
positioning: Short in-house sources: SCIP, his thesis, two student theses, Wallace's ZI Round, MIPLIB 2010 (pp. 3, 8); contrasted with diving and LNS (p. 4); new measure not compared with literature measures (pp. 5-6).
writing: Six pages plus ten-page appendix (pp. 3-18); measure in three numbered definitions plus plain reading (pp. 5-6); graded ranking chain (p. 7); time loss in body, not abstract (pp. 3, 7).
limits_future: Stated: time loss (p. 7) and need for a best known solution (p. 6); not addressed: instances where heuristics worsen the integral (Table 2), variability, machine-speed dependence (p. 6); no future work named (p. 7).

method_links.note: Co-signed: four settings are step 1 of Method 4 for an interacting family, with per-instance tables in the appendix; Table 1 also illustrates Misreading 2 (1.0 to 0.61 alone vs 0.44 to 0.47 knocked out); plain geometric means consistent with the era note.

Payoff redefined for a primal component; time to optimality stands beside the new measure and its loss is printed, but not in the abstract. Attribution: the primal integral appears here in 2011, not only in Berthold 2013.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: measure designed for the component's job
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a time-integrated quality measure, normalised by the all-off run; overlaps Heuristic 8, but the step is to design a new measure, not choose among existing ones

transferable: The primal integral, step by step (pp. 5–6): 1. γ(x̃) = |cᵀx̃_opt − cᵀx̃| / max{|cᵀx̃_opt|, |cᵀx̃|}, with γ = 0 if both values are 0 and γ = 1 if their signs differ. 2. p(t) = 1 before the first incumbent. 3. P(T) = Σᵢ p(t_{i−1})(t_i − t_{i−1}) over the times at which the incumbent changes.
Normalise each instance's integral by the all-off run before averaging, so that the reference setting scores exactly 1.00 (pp. 7, 9).
For an interacting family of components, use four settings (all off, group alone, group knocked out, default). This shows contributions that do not add (pp. 6–7).
Print per-instance values and p(t) step charts in an appendix, so that the instances where the component hurts stay visible (pp. 9–18).
Lock test for safe rounding: a variable without down-locks can be rounded down without violating any ≤ row, and one without up-locks rounded up (p. 4).

title: Solving Hard MIPLIB2003 Problems with ParaSCIP on Supercomputers: An Update
contribution: Single uninterrupted ParaSCIP runs solving ds and stp3d, improved bounds for the four open MIPLIB 2003 instances, and the racing ramp-up and communication-point developments (pp. 3, 9, 20).
problem_entry: How to turn supercomputer CPU time into solved hard MIPs (abstract, p. 3); ds and stp3d had needed over ten restarts in 2010 (pp. 3, 5); parallel MIP is hard because sequential progress shrinks trees (p. 5).
key_idea: Wrap SCIP in UG (LoadCoordinator and Solvers over MPI), presolve once and ship subproblems as bound changes (pp. 5-6), with normal or racing ramp-up and dynamic load balancing by collecting mode (pp. 7-8, 10-11).
assumptions: CIP and MIP defined (pp. 3-4); six MIPLIB 2003 instances with per-run data conditions (pp. 9-10, 18); HLRN II, HLRN III and Titan (p. 10); old and new ParaSCIP/SCIP/CPLEX versions (p. 10).
proof_devices: racing winner rule by dual bound with open-node threshold (p. 10)
diversification by 64 meta-settings, random top-level branching and permutations (pp. 10-11)
racing control with fallback to normal ramp-up (p. 7)
collecting mode with relative dual-bound threshold and hysteresis m_p = 1.5 (p. 8)
primitive-node checkpointing (pp. 8-9)
stage-3 communication points (pp. 9, 11)
experiments: One run per configuration, no repetitions or seeds (pp. 10-18): racing vs normal, 4,096 vs 7,168 cores, restarts vs single run, old vs new version; phase split, transfer and idle ratios, core-hours (Tables 1-2, pp. 13-15); failures reported (pp. 9, 18); new bounds (Tables 3-4, pp. 18, 20).
positioning: Credits Bussieck et al. and Bixby et al. 1999 (p. 5), Mitra et al. and Nwana et al. for racing (p. 7), Shinano, Achterberg and Fujie 2008 (p. 8), Ralphs and Xu et al. (p. 5), Fischetti and Monaci and MIPLIB 2010 for variability (pp. 7, 11), Koch, Martin and Pfetsch (p. 5); no criticism.
writing: Threefold contribution with one first-time claim (p. 3); explanations hedged (pp. 11, 13, 18); results told run by run (pp. 16-19); conclusion concedes evaluation is very difficult and ends with three open questions (pp. 18, 20).
limits_future: Evaluation is hard (pp. 18, 20), memory-conservative single run costs more (p. 15), dano3mip unchanged (p. 18), parameters depend on sequential solver version (p. 15); open questions on scaling and Solvers needed (p. 20).

method_links.note: Co-signed: the sequential state-of-the-art solver comes first; more power on an inferior implementation helps little, SCIP's own progress is a main source of the ds speedup, a powerful MIP solver is crucial; step 1 of Method 5.
Time split by phase and by Solver idle ratio, dominant cost named; idle time explains the stp3d gap, core-hours show restarts cost less.

No library and no knock-out from a default; one run per configuration on one named instance; permutations used to exploit variability (racing) rather than measure noise; bears on Misreading 1 and the Roundtable Card's Fischetti contrast.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a portfolio of settings, random top-level branching and permutations raced on the root, the winner chosen by dual bound and open nodes

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fixed hard instance as a cross-version probe
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ds re-solved with every SCIP release, with the parallel parameters re-tuned because the sequential solver's behaviour changed

transferable: Racing ramp-up recipe (pp. 7, 10–11): 1. Grid of meta-settings: four levels each for heuristics, presolve and separation. 2. Random branching at the top two levels, and permutations of rows and columns. 3. Winner: the best dual bound among Solvers with enough open nodes. 4. Fallback: normal ramp-up if the winner has too few nodes.
Load balancing on a relative dual-bound threshold for good nodes, with hysteresis: on below p, off above 1.5·p (p. 8).
Report a parallel run as a phase split (racing, ramp-up, ramp-down), with the transfer ratio, the idle-time ratio per rank and core-hours (Tables 1–2, pp. 13–15).
Confirm an optimality claim reached through restarts by one uninterrupted run, and try an independent solver given the optimum (p. 9).
Re-run a fixed hard instance with every new release of the sequential solver, and re-tune the parallel parameters to its behaviour (p. 15).
coauthors: Yuji Shinano, Timo Berthold, Stefan Heinz, Thorsten Koch, Michael Winkler

quotes.text: it is crucial to exploit a powerful MIP solver in parallelization
